Multinomial and conditional logit regression

Source: R/estimators.R
mnl.Rd

Fits the multinomial logit (case-specific covariates, alternative-specific coefficients), the conditional logit (alternative-specific covariates, generic coefficients), or their combination by maximum likelihood, with alternative-specific constants, varying choice sets, frequency weights, offsets, unit fixed effects, and analytic, robust, cluster-robust, or bootstrap standard errors. This is the baseline for imnl() and the model the tests of IIA (hausman_mcfadden(), small_hsiao(), fp_tests()) take.

Usage

mnl(
  formula,
  data,
  id = NULL,
  alt = NULL,
  ref = NULL,
  weights = NULL,
  offset = NULL,
  fe = NULL,
  bias_correct = c("none", "jackknife"),
  se = c("analytic", "opg", "robust", "cluster", "bootstrap", "none"),
  cluster = NULL,
  nboot = 200L,
  cores = 1L,
  start = NULL,
  maxit = 1000L,
  reltol = 1e-10,
  firth = FALSE,
  prior = NULL
)

Arguments

formula

A formula; see the section "Two data layouts" of mnl().

data

A data frame.

id, alt

For the long layout, the names of the case and alternative columns of data. Leave both NULL for the wide layout.

ref

The base (reference) alternative: a level of the response. Default: the first level.

weights

Optional frequency weights: a column name in data or a numeric vector with one entry per row (constant within a case in the long layout).

offset

Optional offset on the utility scale: in the long layout a column name or a vector with one entry per row; in the wide layout an \(n \times J\) matrix (columns in level order).

fe

Optional column name in data identifying units that receive alternative-specific fixed effects.

bias_correct

With fe: "none" (default) or "jackknife", the split-panel jackknife of Dhaene and Jochmans (2015) for the slopes; see the fixed-effects section.

se

Standard errors: "analytic" (inverse observed information, default), "opg" (inverse outer product of the scores, the BHHH form that mlogit reports for the nested logit and HEV), "robust", "cluster" (needs cluster), "bootstrap" (nonparametric over cases, or over clusters when cluster is given, with nboot refits from the full-sample estimate; the replicates are kept in object$boot and confint() can report percentile intervals), or "none". With fe, the bootstrap resamples units (a unit drawn twice counts as two units, each with its own fixed effects; a case bootstrap would give units random numbers of cases and a second incidental-parameters bias) and covers the slopes only: the alternative-specific constants and the unit dummies refer to reference units that change between replicates, so their bootstrap standard errors are NA, and first_difference() refuses intervals that need them (use analytic, robust, or cluster standard errors for those). A replicate whose fixed effects cannot be built (an alternative left unconnected to the base) counts as failed, the standard errors are then conditional on resamples in which they can be built, and the fit stops when fewer than half the replicates are usable. A cluster given with fe must nest the units (whole units are drawn; one that cuts across units is refused). The replicates are not jackknife-corrected.

cluster

Optional cluster identifier (a column name in data or a vector aligned to its rows, constant within a case); supplying it selects se = "cluster" unless se is given explicitly.

nboot

Number of bootstrap refits for se = "bootstrap" (default 200).

cores

Number of parallel workers for the bootstrap (a PSOCK cluster; default 1). set.seed() before the call makes the resamples reproducible; serial and parallel runs use different random streams.

start

Optional starting values: the full parameter vector in the order of coef() but on the INTERNAL scale, which differs from coef() for the structural parameters (the logarithms of the inclusive values, scales, and standard deviations; the free Cholesky elements with a log diagonal for the multinomial probit covariance). object$theta of an earlier fit is on that scale. Rarely needed for mnl(), whose log-likelihood is globally concave; the other estimators start from the mnl() estimates (and imnl() from a multistart grid), so start serves to probe another basin of a non-concave likelihood.

maxit, reltol

Controls for the BFGS stage passed to stats::optim() (the plain mnl() is solved by damped Newton steps first, with BFGS as the fallback); the Newton polish that follows runs up to 25 further iterations with the analytic Hessian of the logit family or central differences of the analytic gradient otherwise.

firth

If TRUE, Firth's penalized likelihood (see the section "Penalized (Firth) estimation"); default FALSE, maximum likelihood. Weights are read as frequency weights and must total more than 2.

prior

Optional: priors for the coefficients, made by coef_prior() (normal, Cauchy or t, centred at zero, on coefficients scaled to their columns); the fit is the posterior mode, a penalized fit like firth = TRUE (profile intervals, penalized likelihood-ratio tests, the separated coefficients in separation). Not with firth = TRUE or unit fixed effects.

Value

An object of class c("mnl", "choicemodel"): a list with coefficients, vcov, loglik, fitted.values (the \(n \times J\) matrix of choice probabilities, rows named by case), converged, boundary, ill_conditioned, singular, n_modes, search, start_logliks, the estimation data, and the design used by the methods. See summary.choicemodel(), predict.choicemodel(), first_difference(), rrr(), fit_stats().

Details

With case \(i\), alternatives \(j = 1, \dots, J\) (the levels of the response), base alternative \(b\), and availability \(a_{ij}\), $$V_{ij} = o_{ij} + x_i'\beta_j + w_{ij}'\gamma, \quad \beta_b = 0, \qquad P(y_i = j) = \frac{a_{ij} e^{V_{ij}}}{\sum_k a_{ik} e^{V_{ik}}}.$$ \(x_i\) are the case-specific covariates, \(w_{ij}\) the alternative-specific covariates, \(o_{ij}\) an offset: McFadden's (1974) conditional logit, with the multinomial logit as the case \(w = 0\) (Train 2009, chapter 3). The alternative-specific constants are the coefficients of an intercept in \(x_i\): the formula's intercept in the wide layout, the first part's in the long layout (section "Two data layouts"). The coefficients are reported as "<alternative>:<term>" for \(\beta_j\) and "<term>" for \(\gamma\).

Two data layouts

Wide (one row per case): data is a plain data frame, the response is the chosen alternative (a factor, or integer codes; a character vector is refused because its alphabetical order is rarely the intended one), and the formula is y ~ x1 + x2. All alternatives are available to every case.

Long (one row per case-alternative pair): give id (the case column) and alt (the alternative column; its levels define the alternatives). The response is the 0/1 (or logical) choice indicator, exactly one per case. The formula has up to two parts separated by |: choice ~ w1 + w2 | x1 + x2, alternative-specific covariates first (generic coefficients; the intercept of this part switches the alternative-specific constants on, 0 + switches them off), case-specific covariates second (they must be constant within a case). Alternatives without a row for a case are unavailable to it. An alternative-specific coefficient on an alternative-specific variable is the interaction with the alternative factor, w:alt.

The constants follow the first part only:

  • choice ~ w, choice ~ w | 1 and choice ~ w | x have them;

  • choice ~ 0 + w, choice ~ w - 1 and choice ~ 0 + w | x do not.

The second part's intercept has no effect. | 1 is an empty case-specific part (constants only, when the first part has them), and | 0 does not drop the constants, unlike in mlogit (a message says so). The wide-layout formula y ~ x1 + x2 is the second part alone, its intercept giving the constants (y ~ 0 + x1 drops them).

Missing values, weights, standard errors

Rows with a missing value in any model variable (or in weights, offset, cluster, fe) are dropped before fitting; in the long layout a missing value on any row of a case drops the whole case (a message gives the count), and cases left with a single available alternative are dropped too, as are cases of weight zero. object$data holds the retained rows. weights are frequency weights throughout: a fit with weight 2 equals a fit on duplicated cases in the estimates, the model-based standard errors, the robust and cluster sandwiches (meat \(\sum_i w_i s_i s_i'\)), the information criteria (the weight total is \(n\)), the Vuong and likelihood-ratio statistics, the IIA tests (except the Small-Hsiao test, whose half-samples balance cases rather than weight), the averaged quantities of interest, and the bootstraps (se = "bootstrap" draws multinomial replicate weights with the weight total as size, over units for remnl(); with a cluster the clusters are drawn and carry their rows' weights; boot_pvalue() and boot_lr_test() expand the data to one row per case and need integer weights). Non-integer weights are accepted as frequency weights (a message says so). Survey (probability) weights are NOT supported: the point estimates would be the pseudo-maximum-likelihood ones, but the sandwich needs \(\sum_i w_i^2 s_i s_i'\) and the information criteria, tests, and bootstraps have no design-based meaning (the cluster sandwich with the primary sampling units as clusters, \(\sum_g (\sum_{i \in g} w_i s_i)(\sum_{i \in g} w_i s_i)'\), has the with-replacement linearization form, but strata and finite-population corrections are not handled). se = "robust" is the sandwich over cases, se = "cluster" over clusters (no small-sample degrees-of-freedom adjustment, as in the iop and underdisp packages; Stata's vce(cluster) for maximum-likelihood commands multiplies by \(G/(G-1)\)). nobs() returns the number of cases; logLik() carries the weight total as its nobs attribute, which is what BIC() uses.

Unit fixed effects

fe = "<unit column>" (the name of the column identifying the units, such as fe = "country") adds an alternative-specific constant per unit: one dummy per unit in every non-base equation. A unit that never chooses alternative \(j\) has that constant at \(-\infty\); the limiting likelihood treats \(j\) as unavailable to that unit, which is what the fit does (with a message), and cases left with a single alternative drop out (a captive choice says nothing about preferences and does not count as a choice; as dropping cases can change what a unit chose, the rule and the drop are repeated until nothing changes). A unit that chose a single alternative therefore drops out entirely. A unit that never chooses the base likewise has the base unavailable; its constants are then identified only up to a common shift, so one of its dummies is omitted. The common constant of alternative \(j\) refers to a reference unit: the first unit (in level order) that chose both \(j\) and the base, or else one that links \(j\) to an alternative already anchored; an alternative whose choosers are not connected to the base in this way has no identified constant, and the fit stops and names it. Without alternative-specific constants (a formula with - 1) there is nothing to anchor, and every unit keeps all its dummies (one fewer for a unit that never chose the base). The dummies are dense columns, so a fit with thousands of units and many cases needs memory for an \(nJ \times\) (units \(\times\) alternatives) matrix. Maximum-likelihood unit constants carry the incidental-parameters bias when units have few cases (the fit warns below a median of 10). For short panels the alternatives are the jackknife correction below and the correlated-random-effects model: remnl() on the formula and data that mundlak() returns (the pooled mnl() fit of the same formula gives population-averaged slopes, attenuated towards zero).

bias_correct = "jackknife" removes the leading \(1/T\) term of that bias from the slopes by the split-panel jackknife (Dhaene and Jochmans 2015, Review of Economic Studies): the model is refit on the first and second halves of every unit's cases (rows are split in the order supplied, which should be temporal order; a unit with an odd number of cases contributes both possible splits, averaged) and the corrected slope is 2 * full - mean(halves). Alternative-specific constants and the unit dummies are left at their maximum-likelihood values, as are the log-likelihood, fitted(), residuals(), and the standard errors; coef(), predict(), rrr(), confint(), and first_difference() use the corrected slopes together with the ML constants. The ML slopes are kept in $uncorrected and the half-panel estimates in $jackknife. The identity requires the two halves to estimate the same parameter (time homogeneity), so the correction is REFUSED, with a warning naming the check and the ML fit returned, when the half-panel slopes disagree beyond 2.5 times the mean disagreement of five placebo splits, random halves of every unit's cases that ignore the time order (a regime change), or when the full fit's residuals trend with the within-unit time order for some alternative (an omitted trend, at the 1 percent level with a Bonferroni correction over alternatives: put a time control in the formula, a trend rather than period dummies, which are not identified within the half panels). The placebo splits have the time split's structure (all units, halves of the same lengths), so under time homogeneity the ratio of the two disagreements is centred near 1 at every panel length, while a mid-panel regime change separates the time halves and is balanced in every random split; the splits come from fixed seeds and do not disturb the caller's random-number stream. The constant 2.5 is the smallest of 1.25, 1.5, 1.75, 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5, and 4 that kept the refusal rate of time-homogeneous panels at or below 5 percent at T = 6, 10, and 20 in a calibration Monte Carlo (150 units, J = 3), under a rule written down before that run, and the choice is checked on fresh seeds (verification/jackknife_gate_mc.R and jackknife_gate_holdout.R in the repository, results in the verification ledger). In those simulations a regime change was refused in 92 percent of the panels at T = 6 and in all of them at T = 10 and 20, and an omitted trend in all panels at T = 10 and 20 but only about half at T = 6. A refusal leaves $bias_correct at "none" and the reason in $jackknife_refused, which summary() prints, so that a refused correction cannot pass for a corrected one. It warns when the median panel length is below 6 or the implied correction is large. The correction removes the leading \(1/T\) term only: in the same simulations it over-corrects at T = 6 and 10 (the corrected slopes keep a fraction of the maximum-likelihood bias, with the opposite sign), yet it lowers the root mean squared error and brings the coverage of Wald intervals (with the maximum-likelihood standard errors) closer to nominal at every T studied.

Fit-quality flags

Every fit carries converged (FALSE when the optimizer stopped short or at a saddle, where the log-likelihood rises along a direction in which the Hessian curves upward; a near-zero curvature along which it does not rise, as on the flat ridge of an unidentified model, is not a saddle. At a saddle the fit restarts from the point where the log-likelihood rose most along that direction, up to three times, with a message when that reaches a higher maximum; the saddle warning stays when it does not), diverging (the names of the diverging coefficients), phi_boundary (an inflated fit's split equation at one regime) and saddle, boundary (a structural parameter at zero or infinity, a split equation that puts every case in one regime, or diverging coefficients: separation, or a unit constant at infinity; in mnl() and rologit() fits without unit fixed effects separation is decided exactly by the linear program of separation(), elsewhere a coefficient counts as diverging when its standardized size exceeds 15 and its Wald |z| is below 1.96), ill_conditioned (a singular or nearly singular information matrix; rcond holds its reciprocal condition number, taken on the matrix scaled to a unit diagonal, and singular is TRUE when that number is below 1e-13 or the matrix could not be inverted, and a generalized inverse took its place), and n_modes, the number of distinct local maxima the search found. Every end of the search (one for a single start; for the multistart fits every polished start) is classified by the rules of these flags: a point with a diverging coefficient, a structural parameter at zero or infinity, or a split equation at one regime is a boundary, not a maximum, and so are a saddle and an end that did not converge. Two ends are the same point when their log-likelihoods differ by less than 0.01 and either their estimates differ by less than a tenth of a standard error or every fitted probability by less than 1e-4: ends at other estimates with the same probabilities lie on a ridge where the data do not identify the estimates, and detail says how many ends joined the point that way. Maxima whose information matrix is ill-conditioned are one point when their log-likelihoods differ by less than 0.01, whatever their estimates (a nearly flat direction lets the search stop anywhere along it), and detail counts those ends too; two different maxima of that kind at one height would be counted once, and only the highest end's estimates are kept. search lists the distinct points (loglik, type: "maximum", "boundary", "saddle" or "not converged", reached: the number of ends there, reported, detail), and the rows of search_theta hold their estimates on the internal scale of start; start_logliks and screen_logliks hold the log-likelihoods of every polished and every screened start. n_modes is 0 when no end is a local maximum (the reported fit then carries one of the flags above). Each raises a warning or message at fit time; summary.choicemodel() prints them and glance.choicemodel() returns them. What they mean for the results: after converged = FALSE neither the estimates nor the standard errors should be used (refit from other start values, or simplify the model); with boundary = TRUE the fit is at a limit (it keeps converged = TRUE when the optimizer met its criterion there): the estimates of the parameters at the boundary and their standard errors are not meaningful, the others usually are, and the restricted model is the one to compare with (the search holds log scales, log inclusive values, the multinomial probit's log Cholesky diagonals and log standard deviations within +/- 8; where the log-likelihood still rises at that bound the warning says so, and the reported log-likelihood is then below the model's supremum, so a comparison with the restricted model understates it); ill_conditioned = TRUE (a reciprocal condition number below 1e-9, or a generalized inverse in the covariance) means some combination of parameters is barely identified and its standard errors are unreliable, and with singular = TRUE some parameters are not identified at all: their estimates and standard errors (from the generalized inverse) are not meaningful, and the summary's footer says so, since their rows in the table look like the others. The information of a model whose parameters are not identified is singular at the maximum itself, and close to it its condition number is of the order of the gradient. A fit whose information is ill-conditioned is therefore brought to a stationary point by a few Newton steps before the flag is set, so that the flag does not depend on how closely the search converged; n_modes > 1 means the reported fit is the highest of several maxima found. The reported fit is the highest end of the search, maximum or not: where it is at a boundary and a lower end is a local maximum, a message says so, and that maximum's row of search_theta refits it as start. An alternative that is never chosen (where another is available) is separation: in mnl() and rologit() fits without unit fixed effects the fit runs and reports it (firth = TRUE or a prior then gives finite estimates), while imnl(), hev(), mnprobit(), remnl() and fixed-effects fits refuse such data, and nlogit() does when the alternative has its own constant or slopes (with generic coefficients only it refuses a nest of which nothing is chosen). Data that overlap can still give very large, imprecise estimates (near separation), which raise no flag: their Wald statistics understate the evidence against zero (Hauck and Donner 1977), so the likelihood-ratio tests of term_test() (type = "lr") and lr_test() are the ones to use there, or firth = TRUE. A fixed-effects fit also carries bias_correct and, when a requested correction was refused, the reason in jackknife_refused.

Penalized (Firth) estimation

Under separation (a covariate, or a combination of covariates, that predicts some choices perfectly; Cook, Niehaus and Zuhlke 2018 for the multinomial logit) the maximum-likelihood estimates do not exist, and the reported ones are where the optimizer stopped. firth = TRUE maximizes the log-likelihood penalized by half the log-determinant of the Fisher information (Jeffreys' prior), \(\ell^*(\theta) = \ell(\theta) + \tfrac12 \log |I(\theta)|\), which for the multinomial and conditional logit is Firth's (1993) bias-reducing estimator (Bull, Mak and Greenwood 2002; Kosmidis and Firth 2011): its estimates are finite under separation and have smaller small-sample bias. The penalty is invariant to the choice of base alternative. It shrinks the fitted probabilities towards equal probabilities, so their averages no longer equal the observed shares (Puhr et al. 2017).

A penalized fit reports loglik, the ordinary log-likelihood at the penalized estimates, and loglik_penalized, the maximized objective; the information criteria and pseudo-R-squared measures built on loglik are not those of maximum likelihood. The standard errors are from the inverse information at the penalized estimates (the robust and cluster sandwiches use the per-case scores plus their share of the penalty's gradient; the bootstrap refits with the penalty). The exact separation check of separation() runs on the data: the names of the coefficients along the separating direction are in separation, printed and announced with a message, since their penalized estimates are then determined largely by the penalty. The penalized likelihood is not always concave and can have more than one local maximum (with a high-leverage covariate, even in a binary logit), so without start the fit runs from zero and from the maximum-likelihood estimate (halved towards zero where the penalty is not finite) and keeps the higher maximum, with a warning when the two runs end at different maxima (start_logliks holds both values, n_modes counts the maxima, and a penalized fit keeps no search). Recommended inference: the profile penalized-likelihood intervals of confint() (its default for a penalized fit) and the penalized likelihood-ratio tests of term_test(), combine_test(), and lr_test() (two penalized fits), which maximize the full model's penalized likelihood under the restriction (Heinze and Schemper 2001, 2002). The tests derived for maximum-likelihood estimates refuse a penalized fit: hausman_mcfadden(), small_hsiao(), fp_tests(), iia_tests(), nested_lm_test(), captivity_test(), vuong(), and boot_lr_test(). firth = TRUE is not available with unit fixed effects, and the other estimators do not offer it (in imnl() and remnl() the penalty tends to minus infinity where the model reduces to the multinomial logit, so it would favour the larger model).

Under separation the penalty decides how large the separated estimates are (Rainey 2016). Jeffreys' prior is one default, justified by bias reduction; prior = coef_prior(...) replaces it with independent normal, Cauchy or t priors centred at zero on coefficients scaled to their columns (Gelman et al.'s 2008 default is coef_prior()), and fits under several priors show how much of a separated estimate comes from the prior. A fit with a prior is a penalized fit in every respect above (two starts, separation, profile intervals, penalized likelihood ratios, the refusals); its covariance is the inverse curvature of the log posterior at the mode. For maximum-likelihood fits of separated data, term_test(), combine_test(), lr_test() and boot_lr_test() compare the suprema of the log-likelihoods (likelihood-ratio tests remain valid under separation where Wald tests do not; Rainey 2024).

Firth, D. (1993). Bias reduction of maximum likelihood estimates. Biometrika, 80, 27-38. doi:10.1093/biomet/80.1.27

Gelman, A., Jakulin, A., Pittau, M.G. and Su, Y.-S. (2008). A weakly informative default prior distribution for logistic and other regression models. Annals of Applied Statistics, 2, 1360-1383. doi:10.1214/08-AOAS191

Examples

set.seed(1)
d <- rmnl(500, beta = cbind(b = c(0.5, -1, 0.8), c = c(-0.3, 0.6, -0.5)))
m <- mnl(y ~ x1 + x2, data = d)
summary(m)
#> Multinomial logit 
#> Call: mnl(formula = y ~ x1 + x2, data = d)
#> Alternatives: a, b, c  (base: a)
#> 
#> Outcome equations (alternative:term):
#>               Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> b:(Intercept)   0.4719     0.1236   3.817 0.000135 ***
#> b:x1           -0.8316     0.1487  -5.592 2.25e-08 ***
#> b:x2            0.7032     0.1314   5.352 8.72e-08 ***
#> c:(Intercept)  -0.3910     0.1625  -2.406 0.016124 *  
#> c:x1            0.8982     0.1622   5.538 3.05e-08 ***
#> c:x2           -0.6328     0.1432  -4.419 9.92e-06 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
#> 
#> Standard errors: analytic. Log-likelihood -413.012 on 6 parameters, 500 cases. AIC 838.02, BIC 863.31.
head(predict(m))
#>           a         b          c
#> 1 0.2371501 0.6758323 0.08701760
#> 2 0.3247436 0.3626646 0.31259189
#> 3 0.3254302 0.4548467 0.21972314
#> 4 0.2356573 0.1010445 0.66329826
#> 5 0.2542398 0.6223149 0.12344533
#> 6 0.0921925 0.8969239 0.01088358
rrr(m)
#>           term   block   rrr lower upper      z  p.value
#>  b:(Intercept) outcome 1.603 1.258 2.043  3.817 0.000135
#>           b:x1 outcome 0.435 0.325 0.583 -5.592 2.25e-08
#>           b:x2 outcome 2.020 1.562 2.614  5.352 8.72e-08
#>  c:(Intercept) outcome 0.676 0.492 0.930 -2.406 0.016124
#>           c:x1 outcome 2.455 1.787 3.374  5.538 3.05e-08
#>           c:x2 outcome 0.531 0.401 0.703 -4.419 9.92e-06
## Firth's penalized likelihood, with profile intervals
mf <- mnl(y ~ x1 + x2, data = d, firth = TRUE)
confint(mf)
#>                    2.5 %      97.5 %
#> b:(Intercept)  0.2284361  0.71111992
#> b:x1          -1.1192064 -0.53902765
#> b:x2           0.4440831  0.95665219
#> c:(Intercept) -0.7070561 -0.07340702
